¶

'''Veneraceæ''' (ven-ẹ-rā′sē-ē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Venus'' (''Vener-''), 5, + ''-aceæ.''] Same as ''Veneridæ.''

'''veneracean''' (ven-ẹ-rā′sē-a̤n), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the ''Veneracea.''

'''II.''' ''n.'' Any member of the ''Veneracea.''

'''veneraceous''' (ven-ẹ-rā′shius), ''a.'' Same as ''veneracean.''

'''venerant''' (ven′ẹ-rant), ''a.'' [< L. ''veneran(t-)s,'' ppr. of ''venerari,'' venerate: see ''venerate.''] Reverent. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|When we pronounce the name of Giotto, our ''venerant'' thoughts are at Assisi and Padua.
{{right|''Ruskin,'' Modern Painters, III. i., 1, note.}}}}

'''venerate''' (ven′ẹ-rāt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''venerated,'' ppr. ''venerating.'' [< L. ''veneratus,'' pp. of ''venerari'' (> It. ''venerare'' = Sp. Pg. ''venerar'' = F. ''vénérer''), worship, venerate, revere; from the same source as ''Venus,'' love: see ''Venus.''] To regard with respect and reverence; treat as hallowed; revere; reverence.

{{smaller block|<poem>While beings form’d in coarser mould will hate
The helping hand they ought to ''venerate.''</poem>
{{right|''Crabbe,'' Works, V. 214.}}}}

{{smaller block|The Venetian merchants, compelled to seek safety in Alexandria, visited the church in which the bones of St. Mark were preserved and ''venerated.''
{{right|''C. E. Norton,'' Church-building in Middle Ages, p. 47.}}}}

='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Worship, Reverence,'' etc. See ''adore.''}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|veneer-moth|6717|venerer}}</noinclude>an old English collectors’ name, given from the coloration, which suggests veneering. {{smaller|''Crambus hortuellus'' is the garden veneer; ''C. pinellus'', the pearl veneer; and ''C. petrificellus'', the common veneer. See cut under ''Crambidæ''.}}

¶'''veneer-press''' (vẹ̄-nēr′pres), ''n.'' A special form of press used to hold veneers in position while being glued to woodwork or furniture. {{smaller|Various complicated forms of screw-clamps and screw-presses are used, some being fitted with steam-pipes to keep the glue soft until the veneer has adapted itself to the irregular surface to which it is to be attached.}}

'''veneer-saw''' (vẹ̄-nēr′sâ), ''n.'' A circular saw for cutting veneers from the solid wood, ivory, etc. It has a thin edge, and is thicker toward the center. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''veneer-scraper''' (vẹ̄-nēr′skrā″pėr), ''n.'' A tool with an adjustable blade for dressing veneers. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''venefical''' (vẹ̄-nef′i-kạl), ''a.'' [< L. ''veneficus'', poisonous (see ''venefice''), + ''-al''.] Same as ''veneficial''.
{{smaller block|All with spindles, timbrels, rattles, or other ''venefical'' instruments, making a confused noise.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Masque of Queens.}}}}

'''venefice†''' (ven′ẹ̄-fis), ''n.'' [< L. ''veneficium'', a poisoning, < ''veneficus'', poisoning, < ''venenum'', poison, + ''-ficus'', < ''facere'', make.] Sorcery, or the art of poisoning. ''Bailey'', 1727.

'''veneficial''' (ven-ẹ̄-fish′ạl), ''a.'' [< L. ''veneficium'', a poisoning (see ''venefice''), + ''-al''.] '''1.''' Acting by poison; sorcerous. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|As for the magical virtues in this plant [the mistletoe], and conceived efficacy unto ''veneficial'' intentions, it seemeth a pagan relick derived from the ancient druids.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., ii. 6.}}}} 2. Addicted to sorcery or poisoning.

'''veneficious''' (ven-ẹ̄-fish′us), ''a.'' [< L. ''veneficium'', a poisoning (see ''venefice''), + ''-ous''.] Same as ''veneficial''.
{{smaller block|To sit cross-legged . . . was an old ''veneficious'' practice; and Juno is made in this posture to hinder the delivery of Alcmæna. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., v. 23.}}}}

'''veneficiously''' (ven-ẹ̄-fish′us-li), ''adv.'' By poison or witchcraft.
{{smaller block|The intent hereof [breaking an egg-shell] was to prevent witchcraft; for, lest witches should draw or prick their names therein, and ''veneficiously'' mischief their persons, they broke the shell, as Delecampius hath observed. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., v. 23.}}}}

'''veneisun†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''venison''.

'''venemous†''', ''a.'' An obsolete spelling of ''venomous''.

'''venenate''' (ven′ẹ̄-nāt), ''v. t.'' [< L. ''venenatus'', pp. of ''venenare'', poison, < ''venenum'', poison: see ''venom''.] To poison; charge or infect with poison. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Poisoned jaws and ''venenated'' stings. {{right|''Middleton'', Solomon Paraphrased, xvi.}}}}
{{smaller block|These miasms . . . are not so energic as to ''venenate'' the entire mass of blood. {{right|''Harvey''. (''Johnson''.)}}}}

'''venenate''' (ven′ẹ̄-nāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''venenatus'', pp.: see the verb.] Infected with poison; poisoned.
{{smaller block|By giving this in fevers after calcination, whereby the ''venenate'' parts are carried off. {{right|''Woodward'', On Fossils.}}}}

'''venenation''' (ven-ẹ̄-nā′sho̤n), ''n.'' [< ''venenate'' + ''-ion''.] '''1.''' The act of poisoning.—'''2.''' Poison or venom. {{smaller block|This ''venenation'' shoots from the eye; and this way a basilisk may impoison. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err.}}}}

'''venene†''' (vē-nēn′), ''a.'' [Irreg. (as adj.) < L. ''venenum'', poison: see ''venom.''] Poisonous; venomous.
{{smaller block|Dry air opens the surface of the earth to disincarcerate ''venene'' bodies, or to evacate them. {{right|''Harvey'', On the Plague.}}}}

'''venenifluous''' (ven-ē-nif′lọ̈-us), ''a.'' [< L. ''venenum'', poison, + ''fluere'', flow: see ''fluent.''] In ''bot.'' and ''zoöl.'', flowing with poisonous juice or venom: as, the ''venenifluous'' fang of a rattlesnake. See cuts under ''Crotalus'' and ''viper''.

'''Venenosa''' (ven-ē-nō′sä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., neut. pl. of LL. ''venenosus'', full of poison: see ''venenose.''] One of three sections into which serpents (''Ophidia'') have been divided, according as they are venomous or otherwise, the other sections being ''Innocua'' and ''Suspecta.'' {{smaller|The definition of the group as having grooved fangs in the upper jaw, followed by smaller solid, hooked teeth, would make ''Venenosa'' nearly equivalent to the ''Proteroglypha;'' but if applied to poisonous snakes at large it would be equivalent to ''Proteroglypha'' and ''Solenoglypha'' together. It is disused now, except as a convenient descriptive term, like ''Thanatophidia.'' Also called ''Nocua.''}}

'''venenose†''' (ven′ē-nōs), ''a.'' [< L. ''venenosus'', poisonous: see ''venenous.''] Full of venom; poisonous, as a serpent; belonging to the ''Venenosa;'' nocuous; thanatophidian.
{{smaller block|Malpighi . . . demonstrates that all such tumours, where any insects are found, are raised up by some ''venenose'' liquor, which, together with their eggs, such insects shed upon the leaves. {{right|''Ray'', Works of Creation.}}}}

'''venenosity†''' (ven-ē-nos′i̤-ti), ''n.'' [= F. ''vénénosité'' = Sp. ''venenosidad'' = Pg. ''venenosidade'' = It. ''venenosità''; < ''venenose'' + ''-ity''.] The property or state of being venenose or poisonous.

'''venenous''' (ven′ē-nus), ''a.'' [< OF. ''veneneux'', F. ''vénéneux'' = Pr. ''venenos'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''venenoso'', < LL. ''venenosus'', poisonous, < L. ''venenum'', poison: see ''venom.'' Cf. ''venenose'' and ''venomous'', doublets of ''venenous''.] Poisonous; toxic.—{{smaller|'''Venenous anthelmintic''', a remedy for intestinal worms, which acts by destroying the parasite, and not by simply expelling it: a vermicide as distinguished from a vermifuge.}}

'''venerability†''' (ven″e-ra-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' [< ''venerable'' + ''-ity'' (see ''-bility'').] The state or character of being venerable.
{{smaller block|The excellence and ''venerability'' of their prototypes.
{{right|''Dr. H. More'', Antidote against Idolatry, viii.}}}}

'''venerable''' (ven′e-ra-bl), ''a.'' [< OF. ''venerable'', F. ''vénérable'' = Sp. ''venerable'' = Pg. ''veneravel'' = It. ''venerabile'', < L. ''venerabilis'', worthy of veneration or reverence, < ''venerari'', venerate, revere: see ''venerate''.] '''1.''' Worthy of veneration or reverence; deserving honor and respect, particularly with a suggestion of age or dignity: as, a ''venerable'' magistrate; a ''venerable'' scholar. In the Anglican Church, specifically applied to archdeacons.
{{smaller block|''Venerable'' Nestor, hatch’d in silver.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 3. 65.}}}}
{{smaller block|See how the ''venerable'' infant lies In early pomp.
{{right|''Dryden'', Britannia Rediviva, l. 110.}}}}
{{smaller block|The world — that gray-bearded and wrinkled profligate, decrepit without being ''venerable.''
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xii.}}}}
'''2.''' Hallowed by religious, historic, or other lofty associations; to be regarded with reverence: as, the ''venerable'' precincts of a temple.
{{smaller block|The place is ''venerable'' by her presence.
{{right|''Shirley'', Maid’s Revenge, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|We went about to survey the generall decays of that ancient and ''venerable'' church.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Aug. 27, 1666.}}}}
{{smaller block|All along the shores of the ''venerable'' stream [the Ganges] lay great fleets of vessels laden with rich merchandise.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Warren Hastings.}}}}

'''venerableness''' (ven′e̤-ra̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being venerable.
{{smaller block|The innocence of infancy, the ''venerableness'' and impotence of old age.
{{right|''South'', Sermons, XI. iv.}}}}

'''venerably''' (ven′e̤-ra̤-bli), ''adv.'' In a venerable manner; so as to excite reverence.
{{smaller block|At the moment I was walking down this aisle I met a clean-shaven old canonico, with red legs and red-tasseled hat, and with a book under his arm, and a meditative look, whom I here thank for being so ''venerably'' picturesque.
{{right|''Howells'', Venetian Life, xxi.}}}}

'''Veneracea''' (ven-e̤-rā′sē-ä), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Venus'' (''Vener-''), 5, + ''-acea.''] In ''conch.'': (''a'') A family of bivalves: same as ''Veneridæ.'' (''b'') A superfamily or suborder of siphonate or sinupalliate bivalve mollusks, represented by the ''Veneridæ'' and related families.

'''Veneraceæ''' (ven-ẹ-rā′sē-ē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Venus'' (''Vener-''), 5, + ''-aceæ.''] Same as ''Veneridæ.''

'''veneracean''' (ven-ẹ-rā′sē-a̤n), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the ''Veneracea.''

'''II.''' ''n.'' Any member of the ''Veneracea.''

'''veneraceous''' (ven-ẹ-rā′shius), ''a.'' Same as ''veneracean.''

'''venerant''' (ven′ẹ-rant), ''a.'' [< L. ''veneran(t-)s,'' ppr. of ''venerari,'' venerate: see ''venerate.''] Reverent. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|When we pronounce the name of Giotto, our ''venerant'' thoughts are at Assisi and Padua.
{{right|''Ruskin,'' Modern Painters, III. i., 1, note.}}}}

'''venerate''' (ven′ẹ-rāt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''venerated,'' ppr. ''venerating.'' [< L. ''veneratus,'' pp. of ''venerari'' (> It. ''venerare'' = Sp. Pg. ''venerar'' = F. ''vénérer''), worship, venerate, revere; from the same source as ''Venus,'' love: see ''Venus.''] To regard with respect and reverence; treat as hallowed; revere; reverence.

<poem>While beings form’d in coarser mould will hate
The helping hand they ought to ''venerate.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Crabbe,'' Works, V. 214.}}}}

{{smaller block|The Venetian merchants, compelled to seek safety in Alexandria, visited the church in which the bones of St. Mark were preserved and ''venerated.''
{{right|''C. E. Norton,'' Church-building in Middle Ages, p. 47.}}}}

='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Worship, Reverence,'' etc. See ''adore.''}}

'''veneration''' (ven-ẹ-rā′shọn), ''n.'' [< OF. ''veneration,'' F. ''vénération'' = Sp. ''veneracion'' = Pg. ''veneração'' = It. ''venerazione,'' < L. ''veneratio(n-),'' veneration, reverence, < ''venerari,'' venerate, revere: see ''venerate.''] '''1.''' The feeling of one who venerates; a high degree of respect and reverence; an exalted feeling or sentiment excited by the dignity, wisdom, and goodness of a person, or by the sacredness of his character, and, with regard to a place, by the sacred or historic associations that hallow it.
{{smaller block|Places consecrated to a more than ordinary ''veneration'', by being reputed to have some particular actions done in them relating to the Death and Resurrection of Christ.
{{right|''Maundrell'', Aleppo to Jerusalem, p. 69.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Veneration'' is the name given to the state of mind comprehending both religious regard and a sentiment drawn out by the more commanding and august of our fellow-beings.
{{right|''A. Bain'', Emotions and Will, p. 92.}}}}
'''2.''' The outward expression of reverent feeling; worship.
{{smaller block|“They fell down and worshipped him,” after the manner of the Easterlings when they do ''veneration'' to their kings.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 45.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''phren.'', the organ of adoration, reverence, or respect for what is great and good. See cut under ''phrenology''. ='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|''Reverence'', ''Veneration'', ''Awe'', etc. See ''reverence''.}}

'''venerative''' (ven′e̤-rā-tiv), ''a.'' [< ''venerate'' + ''-ive''.] Feeling veneration; reverent. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I for one, when a ''venerative'' youth, have felt a thrill of joy at being kindly nodded to . . . by some distinguished personage.
{{right|''All the Year Round'', VIII. 61.}}}}

'''venerator''' (ven′e̤-rā-to̤r), ''n.'' [= F. ''vénérateur'' = Sp. Pg. ''venerador'' = It. ''veneratore'', < L. ''venerator'', one who venerates, < ''venerari'', venerate: see ''venerate''.] One who venerates or reverences.
{{smaller block|<poem>Not a scorner of your sex,
But ''venerator''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}}}

'''venereal''' (vẹ̄-nē′rẹ̄-a̤l), ''a.'' [As ''venere-ous'' + ''-al.''] '''1.''' Of or pertaining to venery, or sexual intercourse: as, ''venereal'' desire.
{{smaller block|No, madam, these are no ''venereal'' signs.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., ii. 3. 37.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Then, swollen with pride, into the snare I fell
Of fair fallacious looks, ''venereal'' trains,
Soften’d with pleasure and voluptuous life.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 533.}}}}
'''2.''' Arising from or connected with sexual intercourse: as, ''venereal'' disease; ''venereal'' virus or poison.—'''3.''' Adapted to the cure of venereal diseases: as, ''venereal'' medicines.—'''4.''' Fitted to excite venereal desire; aphrodisiac.—'''5†.''' Of or pertaining to copper, which was formerly called by chemists ''Venus.''
{{smaller block|Blue vitriol, how ''venereal'' . . . soever, rubbed upon the whetted blade of a knife, will not impart its latent colour.
{{right|''Boyle.''}}}}
'''Venereal carnosity.''' {{smaller|Same as ''venereal warts.''}}—'''Venereal disease,''' {{smaller|a collective term for gonorrhea, chancroid, and syphilis.}}—'''Venereal sore''' or '''ulcer,''' {{smaller|chancre or chancroid: more often the latter.}}—'''Venereal warts,''' {{smaller|acuminate condylomata, or warts situated on the mucous surfaces of the genitals. They were formerly supposed to be caused by a venereal poison, but are not now generally so regarded.}}

'''venereant†''' (vē-nē′rē-an), ''a.'' [< ME. ''venerien'', < OF. ''venerien'' = F. ''vénérien''; as ''venere-ous'' + ''-an.''] '''1.''' Inclined to the service of Venus, or to sexual desire and intercourse.
{{smaller block|<poem>For certes I am al ''Venerien''
In feelynge, and myn herte is Marcien.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 609.}}}}
'''2.''' Amorous; wanton.
{{smaller block|Others fall in love with light Wives—I do not mean ''Venerean'' Lightness, but in reference to Portion.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. vi. 60.}}}}

'''venereate''' (vē-nē′rē-āt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''venereated'', ppr. ''venereating''. [< ''venere-ous'' + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] To render amorous or lascivious.
{{smaller block|To ''venereate'' the unbridled spirits.
{{right|''Feltham'', Resolves, i. 26.}}}}

'''venereous''' (vē-nē′rē-us), ''a.'' [= Sp. ''venéreo'' = Pg. It. ''venereo'', < L. ''venereus'', ''venerius'', of or pertaining to Venus or sexual intercourse, < ''Venus'' (''Vener-''), Venus, sexual intercourse: see ''Venus''.] '''1.''' Lascivious; libidinous; lustful; wanton.
{{smaller block|<poem>Lust is the fire that doth maintaine the life
Of the ''venereous'' man (but sets at strife
The soule & body).</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 119.}}
The male . . . is lesser than the female, and very ''venereous.'' {{right|''Derham'', Physico-Theol., iv. 15, note s.}}}}
'''2.''' Giving vigor for or inclination to sexual intercourse; aphrodisiac: as, ''venereous'' drugs.
{{smaller block|No marvell if he brought us home nothing but a meer tankard drollery, a ''venereous'' parjetory for a stewes.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}

'''venerer''' (ven′ėr-ėr), ''n.'' [< ''venery''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who watches game; a gamekeeper; a hunter.
{{smaller block|Our ''Venerers'', Prickers, and Verderers.
{{right|''Browning'', Flight of the Duchess, x.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
